topic.title: Histograms with unequal class widths and the median from a histogram
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: Usually one 6–9 mark question in the last third of M4: draw on a blank grid, then read a frequency or estimate the median; often paired with stratified sampling.
mustMemorise: frequency = frequency density × class width (the area of the bar)
median from a histogram: find the n ÷ 2-th value by adding bar areas, then interpolate inside that class
notOnThisSpec: Frequency polygons drawn over a histogram

note.title: Histograms with unequal class widths
note.subject: maths
notOnThisSpec: Frequency polygons drawn over a histogram

mustBeAbleTo: Calculate the frequency density of every class
Draw a histogram on a blank grid: sensible scale, vertical axis labelled Frequency density, no gaps between bars
Read a frequency from a bar using frequency = frequency density × class width
Estimate how many values lie in part of a class, assuming an even spread
Estimate the median by adding bar areas up to n ÷ 2 and interpolating inside that class
sheet.howExamined: One multi-part question late in the M4 paper, usually 6–9 marks: draw on a blank grid, then read a frequency or estimate the median. Calculator allowed.
traps: Plotting frequency as the bar height
Leaving the vertical axis unlabelled, or choosing a scale that does not fit the grid
Taking the class midpoint, or the middle of the axis, as the median

workedExamples.stem:
The table shows the journey times, $t$ minutes, of 40 bus journeys on the same route.

| Time ($t$ minutes) | $0 < t \le 10$ | $10 < t \le 15$ | $15 < t \le 25$ | $25 < t \le 45$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency | 4 | 10 | 18 | 8 |

Estimate the median journey time.

steps.working: $n = 40$, so the median is the 20th value.
steps.decision: The question says *estimate the median*, so I find the position $n \div 2$ before I look at the classes.

steps.working: Cumulative frequencies: 4, 14, 32. The 20th value lies in $15 < t \le 25$.
steps.decision: 14 journeys are done by $t = 15$ and 32 by $t = 25$, so the 20th is inside this class.

steps.working: I need $20 - 14 = 6$ more values from the 18 in the class: $\frac{6}{18} \times 10 = 3.33$
steps.decision: Values are assumed to be spread evenly across the class, so I take that fraction of the class *width*, not of the frequency.

options: Because a bar is a rectangle, so its area grows in proportion to its width
Because 18 is the largest frequency in the table
Because the median is always in the third class
whyMenu.explain: Area stands for frequency, so moving a fraction of the way across the class passes the same fraction of its values.

steps.decision: Add the offset to the lower boundary of the class, round sensibly and write the unit. The class midpoint, 20, would earn no accuracy mark.

twin.stem: Same classes; the frequencies are now 5, 9, 16 and 10. Estimate the median journey time.

items.stem: The class $20 < h \le 30$ has frequency 16. What is its frequency density?
items.skill: Calculate frequency density from a frequency and a class width

options.feedback: That is the frequency. With unequal class widths the bar height must be frequency ÷ class width, or the drawing mark is lost.
You multiplied by the width. Frequency density divides the frequency by the width of the class.
You divided the width by the frequency. It is the other way round: 16 ÷ 10.

items.stem: On a histogram two bars are the same height. Bar A is for $0 < h \le 20$ and bar B for $50 < h \le 90$. Which class has more values?
items.skill: Read frequency as the area of a bar

options.text: Bar B, because its class is wider
options.feedback: Frequency = frequency density × class width, so the wider bar holds twice as many values.

options.text: They have the same number of values
options.feedback: Equal heights mean equal frequency densities, not equal frequencies. Multiply each height by its class width.

options.text: Bar A, because narrow bars are denser
options.feedback: Both bars are equally dense; the narrower class simply covers fewer values. Compare areas.

options.text: It cannot be decided without the scale
options.feedback: The widths (20 and 40) settle it whatever the vertical scale is: the areas are in the ratio 1 : 2.

context.setting: A garden centre measures the heights of 60 young apple trees

data.caption: The table shows the heights, h cm, of 60 young apple trees.

parts.stem: On the grid, draw a histogram to show this information.

scheme.for: at least one frequency density correctly calculated (0.3, 1.6, 1.3, 0.3), or a frequency-density column started
scheme.seenIf: working contains any of 6/20, 16/10, 26/20, 12/40 or their values

scheme.for: histogram drawn with correct heights, no gaps between bars, vertical axis labelled Frequency density with a linear scale
scheme.examinerNote: Bars drawn to the frequencies (6, 16, 26, 12) score 0 for this part.

hints: The classes are not all the same width, so the bar height is not the frequency.
Divide each frequency by the width of its class.
Frequency densities: 6 ÷ 20 = 0.3 and 16 ÷ 10 = 1.6; now do 26 ÷ 20 and 12 ÷ 40.
parts.workedSolution: Frequency densities: $6 \div 20 = 0.3$, $16 \div 10 = 1.6$, $26 \div 20 = 1.3$, $12 \div 40 = 0.3$. Draw bars of these heights over their classes with no gaps, label the vertical axis *Frequency density* and the horizontal axis *Height (h cm)*.

commonErrors.feedback: The bars have been drawn to the frequencies. With unequal class widths the height must be frequency ÷ class width; the Summer 2025 report says this scored nothing for the drawing.

parts.stem: Estimate the number of trees that are taller than 40 cm.

scheme.for: half of the 30 < h ≤ 50 class: (50 − 40) ÷ 20 × 26 = 13, or 13 seen

scheme.examinerNote: Follow through from a wrongly drawn histogram when the method is clear.

hints: 40 cm is halfway through the class 30 < h ≤ 50.
Assume the 26 trees in that class are spread evenly across it.
Add every tree in the class 50 < h ≤ 90.
parts.workedSolution: Half of the class $30 < h \le 50$ lies above 40 cm: $\frac{10}{20} \times 26 = 13$. All 12 trees in $50 < h \le 90$ are taller than 40 cm. Estimate: $13 + 12 = 25$ trees.

commonErrors.feedback: You counted the whole of the 30 < h ≤ 50 class. Only the part above 40 cm belongs in the estimate.

parts.stem: Estimate the median height of the trees.

scheme.for: 30th value identified (n ÷ 2) and the class 30 < h ≤ 50 chosen from cumulative frequencies 6, 22, 48
30 + (30 − 22) ÷ 26 × 20, or equivalent interpolation inside their class

hints: There are 60 trees, so the median is the 30th value.
Add the frequencies until you pass 30: 6, 22, 48.
You need 8 more of the 26 values in the class 30 < h ≤ 50; take that fraction of the class width.
parts.workedSolution: $n = 60$, so the median is the 30th value. Cumulative frequencies 6, 22, 48 put it in $30 < h \le 50$. Eight more values are needed from the 26 in that class: $30 + \frac{8}{26} \times 20 = 36.15\ldots \approx 36.2$ cm.

commonErrors.feedback: 40 is the midpoint of the median class, not the median. Interpolate: 8 of the 26 values are still needed, so move 8/26 of the way across the class.
45 is the middle of the axis, not of the data. The median is half of the total area of the bars.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh's answer to "Estimate the median height" for the apple-tree data (frequencies 6, 16, 26, 12 in the classes 0–20, 20–30, 30–50 and 50–90 cm):
studentWorking: There are 60 trees, so the median is the 30th value.
Cumulative frequencies: 6, 22, 48, so the 30th value is in 30 < h ≤ 50.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: She took the midpoint of the median class instead of interpolating. Eight of the 26 values in the class are still needed, so the median sits 8/26 of the way across it.
correction: Values still needed: 30 − 22 = 8 of the 26 in the class.
findTheMistake.feedback: Correct class identified — M1. The midpoint gains no further credit: the interpolation is the second method mark and the accuracy mark follows from it. The Summer 2025 examiners reported that the median from a histogram still defeats most candidates.

prompts.prompt: Two bars on a histogram are the same height. Do their classes have the same frequency?
prompts.answer: Only if the classes are the same width. Frequency is the area of the bar: height × width.

findings.asked: Draw a histogram on a blank grid, then estimate the median from it; a stratified-sampling part followed.
findings.wentWrong: Many scored nothing on the drawing: bars at the frequencies, home-made scales, unlabelled axes. The median part was failed by the large majority and the sampling part was often left blank.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Worked out every frequency density first, chose a scale that used the grid, labelled both axes and interpolated inside the median class.
findings.rule: Frequency density before anything else; the median is half of the area, never the class midpoint.

findings.asked: Interpret a histogram, then use the data in a sampling question.
findings.wentWrong: The majority scored zero on both parts.
findings.rule: Read frequencies as areas: height × class width.

findings.asked: Reverse-read a histogram: one frequency given, find the vertical scale and then the other frequencies.
findings.wentWrong: Answers were all or nothing. Candidates who did not set the scale from the known bar could make no progress.
findings.rule: Find the scale from the bar whose frequency you know, then multiply every other height by its width.

insight.ruleToRemember: Label the vertical axis Frequency density; frequency is the area of the bar; the median is half of the total area, interpolated inside its class — never the class midpoint and never the middle of the axis.
insight.aStarSignal: This question sits in the last third of M4, where most candidates score zero; every mark here is one that the field leaves behind.
